title: Rolling z-score
statement: For each index i ≥ w − 1, output the z-score of prices[i] within the window prices[i−w+1..i]: (p_i − mean) / std, using the population standard deviation of the window (0 if the window is constant). Relative error ≤ 10⁻⁶. One test has prices near 10⁶ with tiny moves, so naive running sums of squares will fail.
hints: O(n·w) recomputation is fine for these sizes; O(n) with running sums is the production version.
E[x²] − E[x]² cancels catastrophically when the level is large and the variance small: shift by a reference value, or use a Welford-style update.
complexity: O(n·w) simple, O(n) with stable running moments

solution.explanation: The trap is numerical: with prices near 10⁶ and moves of 0.01, E[x²] ≈ 10¹² while the variance ≈ 10⁻⁴, so the subtraction loses all significant digits in doubles. Fixes: subtract a reference (the first price) before accumulating, which leaves the variance unchanged; recompute the window's deviations from its mean; or use Welford's update adapted for removal. Same lesson as Part 17's OLS centring: floating point bites hardest when the signal is small relative to the level.
solution.python:
def rolling_z(prices, w):
    out = []
    for i in range(w - 1, len(prices)):
        win = prices[i - w + 1:i + 1]; m = sum(win) / w
        var = sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in win) / w
        out.append(0.0 if var <= 1e-18 else (prices[i] - m) / var ** 0.5)
    return out
